mcqs.question: What is the main advantage polling has over interrupt-driven I/O, despite wasting CPU cycles?
options: Polling uses less total electrical power
Polling works on devices that don't have status registers
Polling automatically frees the CPU to run other processes
Polling has essentially zero latency between the device becoming ready and the CPU noticing, with no interrupt-handling overhead
mcqs.explanation: Polling detects readiness the instant it checks, with no context-switch or handler-dispatch overhead — genuinely lower latency for very fast operations. It typically uses more power (CPU stays fully active), still needs a status register, and does not free the CPU for other work.

mcqs.question: On a single-core system, why does polling for a slow disk operation effectively stall the entire machine?
options: The disk physically disconnects the CPU from other cores during polling
Polling triggers an automatic system reboot
The single core is fully occupied checking the status register in a tight loop, so no other process can run until the device becomes ready
The OS scheduler is disabled while a device is busy
mcqs.explanation: With only one core, a busy-wait loop consumes 100% of the only available CPU resource, leaving nothing for the scheduler to give to other processes until the loop exits. Nothing about disk or network hardware disconnects other cores or disables the scheduler directly — it's simply resource exhaustion.

mcqs.question: In interrupt-driven I/O, what does the CPU do between issuing a command to a device and the device completing it?
options: It halts entirely until the interrupt fires
It continues running other processes or handling other I/O, resuming this device's handling only when the interrupt arrives
It repeatedly polls a secondary status register
It duplicates the command to a backup device as a safety measure
mcqs.explanation: The entire point of interrupt-driven I/O is that the CPU is free to do other useful work during the device's operation, unlike polling. It doesn't halt (that would be no better than polling for utilization) and doesn't poll a secondary register, which would defeat the purpose.

mcqs.question: Pure interrupt-driven programmed I/O still has a cost that DMA specifically eliminates. What is it?
options: The cost of issuing the initial command to the device
The interrupt handler still has to copy each byte or word between the device and memory itself; DMA moves the whole block without CPU involvement in that copy
The cost of the device physically completing its operation
The cost of allocating memory for the transfer
mcqs.explanation: Interrupts solve the waiting problem but not the copying problem — the CPU still executes the data movement instructions in its handler. DMA is specifically about removing the CPU from that copy path, letting a dedicated controller move the block directly. Command issuance, device operation time, and memory allocation are unrelated to what DMA improves.

mcqs.question: A device transfers 500MB of data per operation at high frequency. Which I/O technique minimizes CPU involvement in the data path?
options: Programmed I/O with polling
Interrupt-driven I/O without DMA
DMA — the CPU only sets up and receives one completion interrupt per transfer, regardless of size
All three techniques have identical CPU cost for large transfers
mcqs.explanation: DMA's CPU cost is roughly constant per transfer (setup plus one interrupt) regardless of transfer size, while both polling and interrupt-driven programmed I/O scale CPU involvement with the number of bytes moved — a critical difference at 500MB scale.

mcqs.question: Why must an OS handle cache coherence explicitly when using DMA, even though the CPU isn't doing the data copying?
options: DMA transfers write directly to memory, bypassing CPU caches, so a CPU core could hold stale cached data or have dirty cache lines that conflict with what DMA just wrote or is about to read
DMA transfers automatically update every CPU cache without any OS involvement
Cache coherence is irrelevant to DMA and only matters for multi-threaded code
DMA controllers physically cannot access memory that has ever been cached
mcqs.explanation: Because DMA bypasses the CPU's caches, the CPU's view of memory (via its cache) can disagree with what DMA actually wrote or needs to read, unless the OS explicitly flushes or invalidates the relevant cache lines (or the hardware provides coherent DMA). This is a real, non-automatic responsibility — not something DMA handles on its own.
